prompt: The Ekene casing CSG-958 has an annual usage of 240 joints at a unit cost of 1450, and 60 joints on hand. What annual usage value does ABC rank it by?
options: 87000.000000, the stock on hand times the unit cost, which is the value sitting on the shelf.
1450, the unit cost alone, since ABC ranks the dearest items first whatever their usage.
348000.000000, the annual usage times the unit cost.
370000.000000, the value of the ESP motor, which heads the ranking.
explanation: Annual usage value is annualUsage x unitCost: 240 x 1450 = 348000.000000, rank 2 on the register. The stock on hand times the unit cost is the stock value the slow-moving view reports, which measures a different thing. Ranking by unit cost alone would ignore how much of an item flows through the store. 370000.000000 is ESP-MTR's value at rank 1.

prompt: The total annual usage value of the Ekene register is 1580620.000000. What share of it does the ESP motor ESP-MTR carry?
options: 23.408536 percent, its value of 370000.000000 over the total.
45.425213 percent, the cumulative share once the casing is counted.
22.016677 percent, the share the engine returns for CSG-958 at rank 2.
33.333333 percent, the share of the items that class A holds.
explanation: An item's share is its annual usage value over the total, in percent: 370000.000000 over 1580620.000000 is 23.408536. The cumulative share after rank 2 is 45.425213, and 22.016677 is the casing's own share. 33.333333 is the share of the items that class A holds, a count that would treat a motor and an O-ring kit alike, which ABC exists to avoid.

prompt: Class G cement CEM-G brings the cumulative share from 78.753907 to 83.536840 on the Ekene register, with A to 80 percent and B to 95. What class does it take under each boundary rule?
options: A under at-or-below, and B under include-crossing, the higher class in each case.
B under both rules, since its cumulative share of 83.536840 is above 80 either way.
A under both rules, since the share before it, 78.753907, is below 80 either way.
B under at-or-below, and A under include-crossing.
explanation: Under at-or-below the cumulative share including the item decides: "CEM-G: cumulative share 83.53684% is at or below 95% and above 80%", so B. Under include-crossing the share before it decides: "CEM-G: cumulative share before it 78.753907% is below 80%", so A. Each rule reads a different share, which is why the item that crosses a cut-off is the one they disagree on.

prompt: On the Ekene register, which items take a different ABC class under include-crossing from the class they take under at-or-below?
options: CEM-G only, the one item crossing 80 percent.
CEM-G and LUBE-OIL, the two items whose cumulative shares cross a cut-off.
Every item from rank 7 downward, since include-crossing moves each of them up a class.
None: the rules differ only on an exact cut-off.
explanation: CEM-G crosses 80 percent and LUBE-OIL crosses 95 percent, from 94.197214 to 95.654870. Include-crossing places each crossing item in the higher class: CEM-G A, LUBE-OIL B. Every other item takes the same class under both rules. On a share exactly on a cut-off the two rules agree, because no item crosses a line there.

prompt: Under the Ekene policy (A to 80, B to 95, at-or-below), how many items are class A, and what share of the annual usage value do they hold?
options: 7 items, holding 83.536840 percent, the count under the other boundary rule.
6 items, holding 80 percent exactly, since class A is filled up to its cut-off.
6 items, holding 78.753907 percent of the value.
3 items, holding 63.645911 percent, since class A closes at a third of the items.
explanation: Under at-or-below, class A is ranks 1 to 6, ending with GL-VALVE at a cumulative share of 78.753907. A cut-off is a ceiling for the cumulative share under this rule, so A holds what its items hold and need not reach 80. Seven items and 83.536840 are what include-crossing gives, with CEM-G joining A. The cut-offs are shares of value; no share of items closes a class.

prompt: A stated case has items a and b with the same annual usage value of 10.000000. How does the engine order them, and on what footing?
options: a and b both at rank 1, since two items of equal value share a rank between them.
b at rank 1 and a at rank 2, since a tie is ranked by id with the later id first.
It refuses the case, since a tie in value leaves the cumulative share undefined.
a at rank 1 and b at rank 2: the engine ranks ties by id ascending, a choice it states in its basis.
explanation: The basis reads "annual usage value = annualUsage x unitCost, ranked highest first (ties by id); the cumulative share including the item decides against A 80% and B 95%; compared at 12 significant digits" as it prints on the Ekene call. Ranking a tie by id ascending is the engine's stated choice, and id descending is the alternative. No graded figure depends on it, and a tie in value is ranked with no refusal.

prompt: A stated case has three items worth 80.000000, 15.000000 and 5.000000, so the cumulative shares land exactly on 80 and 95. Under at-or-below, what classes does the engine return?
options: A, B and C: a share exactly on a cut-off stays in the class that cut-off closes.
B, C and C: a share on a cut-off has crossed it.
A, A and B: the item on each cut-off is pulled into the higher class, as include-crossing does.
A refusal: a share may not land on a cut-off.
explanation: The engine's reasons read "P: cumulative share 80% is at or below 80%" and "Q: cumulative share 95% is at or below 95% and above 80%", so P is A, Q is B and R is C. Under include-crossing the same case gives the same classes, since the share before Q is exactly 80 and the share before R exactly 95. Nothing here is refused.

prompt: A policy states A to 80 percent and B also to 80 percent. What does the engine return?
options: The classes, with class B empty, since no cumulative share can lie above 80 and at or below 80.
A refusal: "cutoffs.bPct must be a number above aPct 80 and below 100; got 80".
The classes, with B moved up to 95 percent, the figure the engine holds for a missing B cut-off.
The classes, with A and B merged at 80 percent.
explanation: The B cut-off must lie above the A cut-off and below 100, so a policy that leaves no room for class B is refused before any item is ranked. The engine holds no cut-off of its own and merges no classes; it returns the policy to its author to state again.

prompt: A learner sets the boundary rule control to not stated in the ABC view. What does the engine print?
options: The classes under at-or-below, the rule most textbooks use, with a note that the rule was taken as read.
The classes under both rules side by side, so the learner can pick one after seeing the results printed.
The classes with the crossing items left unclassed until a rule is stated, each flagged in its own reason.
"boundaryRule must be 'at-or-below' (the cumulative share including the item decides) or 'include-crossing' (the share before the item decides, so the item crossing a cut-off joins the higher class)"
explanation: The engine holds no boundary rule: leaving it out is refused with a message that names both rules and what each one decides. It picks neither and prints no side-by-side result. Neither rule is right in general, so a policy picks one and writes it down.

prompt: The engine's basis for ABC cites Caplice, MIT ESD.260J (2006) lecture 11 slide 4. What does the course take from that citation about the cut-offs?
options: The lecture fixes A at 80 percent and B at 95 percent, and the engine applies those two figures to every register.
The lecture prints a table of cut-offs by industry, and the engine reads the oil and gas row whenever it is called.
The classes are arbitrary, so the cut-offs are the caller's stated policy and the course states none as a standard.
The lecture sets the cut-offs by item count, and the engine converts them to shares of value before it classifies.
explanation: The basis reads "Caplice, MIT ESD.260J (2006) lecture 11 slide 4 (standard ABC analysis; the classes are arbitrary, so the cut-offs are the caller's stated policy)". The source supports ranking by value; where the lines fall is a decision the policy writes down. 80 and 95 are the Ekene policy's choice, and the engine refuses a call that states no cut-offs.

prompt: HEAT-TRC, the obsolete heat tracing controller, has an annual usage of 0 at a unit cost of 3100. How does the Ekene ABC run treat it?
options: It is refused, since an item with no annual usage value cannot be placed in the ranking.
It is ranked last with a value of 0.000000 and a cumulative share of 100.000000, class C.
It is ranked by its unit cost of 3100, since its usage of zero would otherwise hide it from view.
It is left out of the ranking and listed apart, with a reason saying it holds no value.
explanation: An item may have zero value; it ranks at the foot of the register, 18th, and is class C under either rule. Only a register in which every item has zero value is refused: "items must carry some annual usage value; every annualUsage x unitCost is 0". The engine ranks by annual usage value alone and leaves no item out.

prompt: PSV-KIT is criticality class V on the Ekene policy. Which ABC class does it take under the Ekene cut-offs and at-or-below?
options: C, since six kits a year at 3800 each carry a cumulative share of 97.097342.
A, since every class V item is also ABC class A.
B, since its safety score lifts its annual usage value by the override weight.
V, since ABC reuses the criticality classes.
explanation: ABC weighs the money that flows through an item: PSV-KIT's value of 22800.000000 ranks 13th and its cumulative share of 97.097342 is above 95, so it is C. Criticality weighs the consequence of a stockout and plays no part in ABC. The two classes answer two questions, which is why the course writes "criticality class V" and "ABC class C".

prompt: BARYTE is criticality class D on the Ekene policy. Where does it sit by annual usage value?
options: Rank 18, class C, since a class D item has the least consequence and carries no weight in ABC.
Rank 5, class B, one below its ranking.
Rank 1, class A, since bulk materials are always ranked ahead of spares by annual usage.
Rank 5, class A, with a value of 78000.000000 from 300 tonnes a year at 260 each.
explanation: BARYTE's annual usage value is 300 x 260 = 78000.000000, rank 5, with a cumulative share of 73.895054, at or below 80, so A. Criticality plays no part in the ranking. It ranks behind ESP-MTR, CSG-958, ESP-PMP and WH-MV on value, and nothing moves an item by its kind.

prompt: What does the cumulative share of GL-VALVE, 78.753907, decide about GL-VALVE under the Ekene policy and at-or-below?
options: It is below 95, so GL-VALVE is class B.
It is within two points of 80, so GL-VALVE is flagged for a boundary review.
It is at or below 80, so GL-VALVE is class A, the last item in A.
It sits near the cut-off, so GL-VALVE is class A only under include-crossing.
explanation: Under at-or-below the cumulative share including the item decides, and 78.753907 is at or below the A cut-off of 80, so GL-VALVE is A, at rank 6. The next item, CEM-G, carries the share past 80. B takes shares above 80 and at or below 95. The engine flags nothing near a cut-off, and compares shares at 12 significant digits with no rounding to whole numbers.

prompt: How many Ekene items are class A under include-crossing, with the same cut-offs of 80 and 95?
options: 7, since CEM-G joins A when the share before it decides.
6, as under at-or-below.
8, since include-crossing also lifts MECH-SEAL, the item after CEM-G.
5, since include-crossing closes A as soon as the share before an item passes 70.
explanation: Under include-crossing ranks 1 to 7 are A: CEM-G's share before it is 78.753907, below 80, so it joins A. MECH-SEAL's share before it is 83.536840, at or above 80, so it is B. Six A items is the at-or-below count. The rule changes which share is read; the cut-offs stay 80 and 95.
